title: Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help?
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022)
problem_statement: Deep multi-task learning models frequently encounter task interference when multiple tasks compete for shared network capacity. Numerous specialized multi-task optimization (MTO) algorithms claim to resolve this interference and outperform simple scalarization, but the empirical validity, reproducibility, and practical benefits of these algorithms remain unverified across realistic benchmarks.
domain: Deep Multi-Task Learning (Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision)
theoretical_framework: Multi-objective optimization and Pareto optimality theory. Under convex optimization principles, linear scalarization is theoretically guaranteed to yield Pareto optimal solutions, and sweeping scalarization weights traces the complete Pareto frontier. The authors evaluate whether non-convex deep multi-task networks require specialized multi-task optimization algorithms to reach the Pareto frontier.
methodology: The authors perform large-scale empirical evaluations comparing specialized multi-task optimization algorithms (MGDA, GradNorm, PCGrad, IMTL, and RLW) with linear scalarization across multilingual machine translation and computer vision benchmarks. The researchers conduct systematic hyperparameter grid searches for learning rates, weight decay, and dropout rates across all optimizers. The study tracks dynamic task weight trajectories during training, evaluates model sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning and evaluation weighting schemes, and compares the computational cost of per-task gradients against model capacity scaling.
datasets: WMT15 English-French (40,853,298 training examples, 4,503 evaluation examples)
WMT19 English-Chinese (25,986,436 training examples, 3,981 evaluation examples)
WMT16 English-German (4,548,885 training examples, 2,169 evaluation examples)
WMT16 English-Romanian (610,320 training examples, 1,999 evaluation examples)
CityScapes (urban scene understanding dataset with 2,975 training, 595 validation, and 500 test images for 7-class semantic segmentation and depth estimation)
CelebA (200,000 celebrity face images annotated with 40 binary attribute classification tasks)
Multi-MNIST (multi-task benchmark with overlaid digit pairs partitioned into 48,000 training, 12,000 validation, and 10,000 test images)

metrics: Cross-entropy loss on validation and training sets
Sacre-BLEU translation quality score via beam search decoding (beam size 4)
Pixel accuracy (%) and Mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) for semantic segmentation on CityScapes
Absolute error and L1 loss for depth estimation on CityScapes
Mean classification error (%) across 40 attribute binary classification tasks on CelebA
baselines: Linear scalarization via proportional batch sampling and static loss weighting
Random Loss Weighting (RLW with Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions)
architectures: Pre-LN Transformer encoder-decoder models (3L-3L base up to 12L-12L, 512 model dimension, 2048 feed-forward dimension, 8 heads, 64K vocabulary)
LeNet convolutional architecture with task-specific fully connected heads (Multi-MNIST)
ResNet-18 shared backbone with 40 task-specific linear heads (CelebA)
ResNet-50 shared encoder with task-specific decoders (CityScapes)

key_findings: Specialized multi-task optimization algorithms fail to improve the performance trade-off curve beyond what simple static scalarization achieves across language translation and vision benchmarks.

Dynamic task weights assigned by MTO algorithms (such as GradNorm, PCGrad, MGDA, and IMTL) remain nearly constant during training, causing these algorithms to behave like static loss weighting in practice.

In low-resource translation settings (English to Romanian), scalarization discovers globally optimal generalization solutions, whereas MTO algorithms converge to near-equal weights that produce suboptimal generalization.

Multi-task neural networks exhibit acute sensitivity to optimization hyperparameters such as learning rate and weight decay; sparse learning rate sweeps produce six to seven times more variance than seed variation, creating misleading illusions of algorithmic superiority in undertuned baselines.

Comparative rankings among MTO algorithms shift substantially when changing the evaluation weighting function, whereas well-tuned scalarization consistently matches or outperforms all MTO algorithms under any evaluation metric.

Computing per-task gradients in MTO methods decreases training throughput from 11.52 to 4.81 steps per second; reallocating this computational budget to scale Transformer model depth strictly improves the Pareto frontier for all task weighting preferences.

Discrepancies in previously reported benchmark results for CelebA and CityScapes stem from undertuned baseline hyperparameters and reporting noisy validation metrics boosted by frequent early stopping.
scope_and_delimitations: Constrained the empirical investigation to supervised multi-task learning benchmarks in natural language translation and computer vision, excluding reinforcement learning and self-supervised pre-training domains.
Focused exclusively on hard parameter sharing architectures (Transformer encoder-decoder, LeNet, ResNet-18, ResNet-50) rather than soft parameter sharing, branched backbones, or modular networks.
Traced Pareto frontiers by performing exhaustive grid searches over static scalarization weights and proportional sampling ratios.
Used beam search with a fixed beam size of 4 without tuning decoding hyperparameters for translation evaluation.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Our results suggest that by exploring the scalarization solution space, one can attain performance on par with (or better than) many MTO algorithms. However, the grid search approach we used for computing the scalarization Pareto frontier is computationally prohibitive.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that identifying the optimal scalarization Pareto frontier requires an exhaustive grid search over task loss weights, which is computationally prohibitive for practical deployment. Furthermore, the empirical study is restricted to supervised multi-task learning tasks and does not evaluate reinforcement learning or self-supervised learning settings.

generalizability_gap: The authors conducted experiments solely on supervised machine translation and computer vision datasets; the authors did not test whether the observed equivalence between scalarization and multi-task optimization holds in reinforcement learning, self-supervised representation learning, speech recognition, or multi-modal foundation models.
methodological_gap: The study relies on exhaustive, computationally expensive grid searches over static loss weights and learning rates to identify the empirical Pareto frontier, rather than developing an automated, single-run optimization algorithm to discover optimal scalarization weights efficiently.
future_work: Developing computationally efficient algorithms and search strategies to navigate the scalarization solution space without prohibitive grid searches.
Establishing the Common Task Framework (CTF) for multi-task optimization to ensure standardized benchmarks, competitive baselines, and rigorous validation/test splits.
Investigating whether the empirical parity between scalarization and multi-task optimization holds in reinforcement learning and self-supervised learning domains.
